title: Day 1 of Division Series delivered no-hit history, a 4-inning save and the latest dome debate
content:
A guy broke up a no-hitter — by making an out! … Another guy hit a ball that looked like a game-winning ninth-inning homer — until a domed stadium had other ideas! … And a closer did something in October that even Mariano Rivera has never done!

If all that sounds like the kind of stuff somebody should write about, it’s a good thing we invented the postseason Weird and Wild column, because I just did that. So let’s dive into the wackiness from Day 1 of the Division Series, starting with a game in Tampa Bay that was …

When Tampa Bay Rays ace Drew Rasmussen jogged to the mound before the eighth inning Saturday, history was in the air. We love it when that happens.

Six outs from no-hit glory … the mighty New York Yankees on the other end of it … and a manager (Kevin Cash) who seemed willing to let his most trusted starting pitcher actually try to take this to the finish line.

So we were headed for a weird, wild, exhilarating finish, all right. Just not the one we had in mind.

Of all the scenarios you could have imagined for the demise of this no-hit dance, I’m thinking this wouldn’t have been in your top 1,000 guesses:

A catcher (poor Austin Wells) chugging his way into getting thrown out at third trying for a triple … for the dagger of a third out … in the eighth inning of a one-run game? That went well.

So how weird and wild was that? Let’s spin that question around the blender and see what pours out.

It’s a hit … you’re out! We need to begin with the nuttiest note we unearthed. Think about this:

A pitcher loses a no-hitter in the eighth inning … on a “hit” in which the batter also made an “out”?

C’mon. That’s practically impossible.

Oh, it happened. Wells got credit for a double, even though he ran into one of the most ill-advised outs at third base in postseason history. But that’s not in dispute. It’s not even the weird and wild part.

The weird and wild part is this: There’s almost no precedent for a no-hitter getting busted up that way in modern times.

I ran this past my friends from STATS Perform. They found a staggering 532 no-hit bids (including this one) that were broken up in the eighth inning or later since 1974, in the regular season and postseason. How many of those would you think ended on a “hit” in which the batter wound up being “out?”

The lucky number actually isn’t zero for a change. But it’s the next-best thing — because it’s happened precisely once.

And that was 46 years ago …

And also in the eighth inning of a game in which the Yankees were being no-hit … on the road … and losing 1-0.

Because the baseball gods wouldn’t have it any other way.

In that game, Lou Piniella (who would later manage the Rays, naturally) was the hitter. Steve Trout was the pitcher (for the White Sox). It was July 13, 1980. And the good news for the Yankees was that Piniella wiped out Trout’s no-hit bid with a single. But the bad news was he got thrown out trying to hustle into second.

That, however, was it for the complete list of no-hitters broken up despite the hitter making an out … until it happened again on a scintillating Saturday in October nearly a half-century later.

Baseball. Does it make any sense at all?

A no-hitter almost disappeared on a triple … by a catcher! OK, imagine an alternate universe in which Wells was somehow safe at third. I tried living in that universe briefly just so I could ask:

How many times has a no-hitter bitten the dust on a late-inning triple by a catcher?

I’m thinking you can guess this one. Complete, reliable, public play-by-play data goes back to 1974. And in all that time, according to STATS, not a single no-hitter has been broken up on a triple by a catcher — in the eighth inning or later, regular season or postseason.

Matter of fact, only one postseason no-hit bid has ever been broken up by a catcher — on any kind of hit — in the eighth or later. It was Ernie Lombardi, who did it as recently as 87 years ago, by singling to pull the plug on a no-hitter by Monte Pearson in the 1939 World Series. And who did Pearson pitch for? The Yankees, of course.

Rasmussen almost pulled a Johnny Vander Meer! One other wild storyline we wouldn’t want to overlook is that it’s been a while since a pitcher twirled a complete-game no-hitter against the Yankees. Here’s how long a while it’s been:

Since the last time it happened — Sept. 20, 1958 (Hoyt Wilhelm) — all other teams have had 168 complete-game no-hitters thrown against them, just in the time during which the Yankees had none. I realize I’m ignoring some famous combined no-hitters against the Yankees in that span, but it’s my column, so I make up these rules.

And they almost didn’t matter anyway, because Rasmussen nearly rewrote that bizarre chapter in no-hit history — twice.

Wait. Twice? Yes, twice. It wasn’t just in this start. In his previous start — on Sept. 22 at Yankee Stadium — he took a no-hitter into the seventh inning. And even though he didn’t complete either one, how could I not ask the folks at STATS:

How many pitchers have taken a no-hitter into the seventh inning against the Yankees in back-to-back starts?

I knew it wouldn’t be many. And the answer is exactly one since 1974: a fellow named Drew Rasmussen.

In fact, it’s so rare for a starting pitcher to take back-to-back no-hitters into the seventh, against any team, that STATS reports he’s only the second starting pitcher in the last 30 years to do it in the same season. The other was Justin Verlander, who did it in consecutive 2022 starts against the Twins — the first in May, the second in August.

But to find the last pitcher before Rasmussen to do that, in consecutive starts against any team in the same month, you would have to go back to July 1992, when Ron Darling flirted with two no-hitters against the Blue Jays.

So sure, it would have been way cooler if Rasmussen had actually completed his postseason no-hitter and lined up alongside Don Larsen and Roy Halladay. But on the other hand, since that isn’t how it turned out, we got to drop names ranging from Piniella to Lombardi to Darling. And without all that eclectic name-dropping, it wouldn’t be the Weird and Wild column, now would it?

Grant Taylor obviously never read the Lee Smith Handy Dandy Guide to Keeping Your Saves Short and Sweet.

A four-inning save? In October? These days, we’re ready to throw a parade for guys who get a four-out save. But after four outs, the closer for those Chicago White Sox is just breaking a sweat.

In his team’s 3-0 Game 1 win Saturday in Cleveland, Taylor spun off just the sixth postseason save of four innings (or more) since the modern save rule arrived in 1969. So he’ll get to hang out with Madison Bumgarner (2014), Vida Blue (1972), Pedro Borbón (1976), Sammy Stewart (1983) and Lance McCullers Jr. (2018) any time that Four-Inning Save Club throws a reunion. However …

Taylor’s stunning little 42-pitch, 13-batter, six-punchout save was even wilder (and weirder) than that list would make you think. Here’s why.

This game was way too close for a marathon save! Those of us who geek out on three-inning and four-inning saves know the formula. A team finds itself leading, 17-3, after six innings … somebody has to finish it … and it’s better if that’s an actual relief pitcher than, say, Luisangel Acuña.

But that was not the formula the White Sox used in this game. They held just a 2-0 lead when Taylor arrived on the mound in the sixth inning and were still ahead by only three runs heading to the ninth. So …

This was only the third save of four-plus innings in a game that close in modern postseason history (since 1969). Here come the others:

Madison Bumgarner (5 IP) — Game 7, 2014 World Series
Vida Blue (4 IP) — Game 5, 1972 ALCS

So that’s two starting pitchers who did that, both in winner-take-all games … as opposed to a team’s closer who did it Saturday in a Game 1. Amazing.

He outlasted the starter! The White Sox starter/opener in this game (Hagen Smith) got eight outs. But the guy who saved this game (Taylor) got 12 outs? You don’t see that parlay much.

In fact, Taylor became only the second pitcher since 1969 to go four innings (or more) for a postseason save while collecting more outs than the guy who started for his team that day. The other came in the MadBum Game (Game 7 of the 2014 World Series):

(Source: Baseball Reference / Stathead)

Eleven Ks in two games! Two appearances into Taylor’s postseason, he’s writing a script all his own. In his first outing, in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, his line was 7 outs, 5 Ks, one game finished. In this one, he spun off an even more seldom-seen line: 12 outs, 6 Ks, another game finished.

So that’s 11 strikeouts and two games finished over two consecutive appearances? I don’t want to give you the impression that’s never happened in the postseason, but I’m pretty sure no living humans would remember the other two pitchers to do this:

STRUCK OUT 11+ IN CONSECUTIVE POSTSEASON GAMES, FINISHED BOTH

(Source: Baseball Reference / Stathead)

So let’s hear it for the closer for these 2026 White Sox. It’s like he rode a time machine to these games, as opposed to the team bus. And this column is eternally grateful for his help in getting us through another day of quadrupleheader weirdness and wildness.

There’s something about Milwaukee in October. The leaves change colors. The Packers change running backs. And the Brewers magically make home runs disappear.

Last October in Milwaukee, I watched Max Muncy hit a rocket to the center-field wall in the NLCS that sure looked like a grand slam, but somehow turned into a 404-foot “ground-ball” double play that never actually hit the ground.

So that was weird. And also wild. But was it weirder or wilder than what happened in the ninth inning Saturday night? I don’t even know anymore.

This October’s Milwaukee magic trick went like this: Ty France pounded a ball 105 mph off the bat, with a NASA-esque 49-degree launch angle, that sure looked like it was going to be a game-winning home run, except …

It inexplicably got swatted downward by the roof of American Family Field … into Jackson Chourio’s waiting glove? Unbelievable. And here I thought the world’s largest pinball parlor, Tropicana Field, was the nuttiest domed stadium in history.

So where does this rank among the wackiest havoc ever wreaked by domes on innocent baseballs? The Weird and Wild column would like to present its favorite entries in that debate through the years.

Long live the Kingman — On May 4, 1984, Oakland’s always-innovative Dave Kingman hit a ball that got stuck in the Metrodome roof in Minnesota. He got a ground-rule double out of it. But it also made Kingman an official violator of one of nature’s most sacred laws — that what goes up must come down. Ha. Not in the Metrodome, it didn’t.

But that isn’t even the weird and wild part. That part involves the Twins’ sneaky plot the next day to exact their revenge by sending a worker up to retrieve the ball. He was supposed to drop it to the Twins’ first baseman, Mickey Hatcher, who was going to catch it and tag Kingman out retroactively. Only one minor problem: When the ball returned to earth, it hit Hatcher on the head.

“At least it hit him where it couldn’t hurt him,” quipped his manager, Billy Gardner.

Trop till you drop — I don’t even know where to start recounting all the nuttiness wafting from the roof of Tropicana Field, home of the Rays. According to their official count, more than 200 fair balls have collided with the four catwalks dangling from the roof of the Trop. And they, too, have had issues with the law of gravity.

The first batter to learn that firsthand was fabled Devil Rays slugger Jose Canseco. On May 2, 1999, he hit a ball that soared way up toward the heavens … until it got stuck in one of those pesky catwalks. So Canseco proposed a new ground rule.

“I think if a ball gets stuck up there, you should take as many bases as you can get,” he said. “You might get 10 or 12 runs until they figure out how to get up there and get the ball.”

He also predicted: “That may never happen again.” So of course, a mere 20 days later, he did it again!

Houston, we had a speaker problem — The great Mike Schmidt hit 548 home runs for the Phillies. The hardest ball he ever hit wasn’t one of them.

That’s because he hit it in Houston, at baseball’s original dome, the Astrodome. On June 10, 1974, Schmidt launched a ball so high and so far that it hit a speaker 117 feet above the field and 329 feet from the batter’s box. A Houston physicist later estimated it would have gone 500 feet if the speaker hadn’t gotten in the way.

But that didn’t help Schmidt. He was already in the middle of his home run trot when the ball came crashing straight down into center field, where Cesar Cedeno scooped it up and held Schmidt to the longest single of his career.

If it makes Schmidt feel better, Cedeno said afterward: “I’ve never seen a ball hit so far in my life.”

No soup for you — My final wacky Dome memory happened during the 1991 Home Run Derby in Toronto, when a big strong dude named Cecil Fielder pounded two home runs that disappeared — not into the roof of what was then the Skydome, but into the Sightlines bar — located way, way, wayyyy out there in the third deck in center field.

And why do I mention those homers now? Only because they produced my favorite Home Run Derby quote ever, from the late, great Dave Henderson.

After the Derby, I found Henderson at his locker in the American League All-Star clubhouse and told him I’d trekked all the way out to Sightlines to talk to the folks who were shocked to see a home run ball bearing down on their tables.

Henderson’s response: “Ever heard that saying, ‘There’s a fly in my soup’? Well, there was a fly ball in that guy’s soup.”

I don’t know what that has to do with France’s home run that wasn’t in Milwaukee on Saturday. But it’s my Weird and Wild column. So there’s never a bad time to drop that quote into it.

1. Maxed out — Nobody in history has hit more postseason home runs for the Dodgers than Max Muncy (17). You probably knew that. What you didn’t know is this: He has hit a home run in the same postseason game as 12 other Dodgers: Chris Taylor, Joc Pederson, Justin Turner, Kike Hernández, Teoscar Hernández, Will Smith, Cody Bellinger, Corey Seager, Edwin Rios, Trea Turner, Miguel Rojas and now Kyle Tucker. What a list.

2. For starters — I’m not sure where this postseason trail will lead the White Sox. I’m just fascinated by the idea of a team trying to win a World Series while dispensing with the whole concept of “a starting rotation.” How different is this White Sox team from the last White Sox team to win a postseason series back in 2005? That year, no White Sox starter got fewer than all 27 outs in the ALCS. Meanwhile, this year, their starters have combined for 29 outs in the whole postseason.

3. One and done — That Rasmussen gem was only the Yankees’ third 1-0 postseason loss in the last 70 years. Want to hear the others? Of course you do.

Game 3, 1963 World Series: Don Drysdale over Jim Bouton
Game 5, 1957 World Series: Lew Burdette over Whitey Ford

4. The Miz Kid — It felt like a rough night in the life of Jacob Misiorowski. And he still threw 52 pitches at 100 mph or faster — in four innings. It also took him two pitches to fire the two fastest pitches ever recorded in a postseason game (104.8 mph on his first pitch, 104.6 on his second). So your new leaderboard of the top five fastest postseason pitches in the Statcast era looks like this:

Miz — 104.8 (Saturday)
Miz — 104.6 (Saturday)
Miz — 104.5 (Saturday)
Mason Miller — 104.5 (Game 2, 2025 NLDS)
Aroldis Chapman — 104.2 (Game 3, 2010 NLDS)

5. All exits don’t look the same — Finally, there were two run-scoring hits in the White Sox-Guardians game. One was a Munetaka Murakami homer that had an exit velocity of 112.2 mph. It was the hardest ball hit by anyone all day.

The other was an accidental double by Colson Montgomery that left the bat at 64.0 mph. There were 37 balls put in play in this game. Montgomery’s double was the 36th-hardest hit. Montgomery had 55 extra-base hits this year. You know how many of those had a harder exit velo than his double Saturday? Right, you are: That would be all 55 of them.

Wild, isn’t it? But they all count exactly the same in …
